blurb.en: Palaces, hill temples and the events that played out inside them.

summary.en: The fortified seat of the Peshwas, founded by Bajirao I in 1730. Its name joins the Marathi words for Saturday and a residence complex.

en.text: Bajirao I laid the foundation on Saturday, 10 January 1730; the opening ceremony was held on 22 January 1732.

Peshwa Narayanrao was killed here in 1773. The East India Company took over the Wada on 17 November 1817, and a fire that began on 27 February 1828 is reported to have burned for seven days.

summary.en: A residence built near the later Shaniwar Wada around 1630. The original was lost long ago; today's building is a municipal reconstruction from the 1980s.

en.text: Lal Mahal was built in 1630 by Dadoji Konddeo, with permission from Shahaji, as part of reviving the recently razed town.
The original building was ruined towards the end of the 17th century and later razed. Its exact site is not known, though it stood very close to Shaniwar Wada.
The present structure was built by the Pune Municipal Corporation between 1984 and 1988. It covers only part of the original land and does not follow the original design.
Lal Mahal is where Shivaji attacked Shaista Khan, who lost four fingers escaping through a first-floor window; Aurangzeb later transferred Shaista Khan to Bengal.

title.en: The earliest names of Pune: competing accounts

summary.en: Encyclopaedia accounts link Pune to early inscriptions that call the area Punaka or Punya vishaya, but they disagree about the dates and the dynasty. PunePedia has not yet read the inscriptions themselves.

en.text: The English Wikipedia article on the history of Pune says that two copper plates dated 758 and 768 CE, issued by the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, refer to the area as 'Puny Vishaya' and 'Punaka Vishaya'. It supports this with an article by M. R. Kantak in the Bulletin of the Deccan College Research Institute.

The article on Pune on the same site attributes plates of 758 and 768 CE to the Yadava dynasty instead. It also mentions plates of 858 and 868 CE naming an agricultural settlement called Punnaka, and a Rashtrakuta inscription of 937 CE naming Punya-vishaya. Most of these statements carry no visible footnote.

Because the two accounts disagree on the dynasty and the dates, no single 'first name' or founding date is presented here as settled. The next step is to read the plate texts in a published edition and record the exact readings.

summary.en: On 5 November 1817 East India Company troops defeated a Maratha army at Khadki. Twelve days later the Company took over Shaniwar Wada.

en.text: The Battle of Khadki (also called Kirkee or Ganeshkhind) was fought on 5 November 1817 between a Maratha force under Bapu Gokhale and East India Company troops under Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Burr, and ended in a Company victory.
The Company took over Shaniwar Wada on 17 November 1817.
Peshwa rule ended in 1818 with the defeat of Bajirao II.
The encyclopaedia page is inconsistent in places (one reference gives the year as 1816). Troop strengths and casualty figures are left out until checked against a primary account.

title.en: Jyotirao Phule founds the Satyashodhak Samaj

summary.en: On 24 September 1873 Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune to oppose caste privilege and widen education and rights.

en.text: The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded in Pune on 24 September 1873 by Jyotirao Phule. Savitribai Phule led its women's section.

Its aims included education and greater social and political rights for women, peasants and Dalits; rejection of caste hierarchy and of priestly intermediaries; and simpler weddings, inter-caste marriage, widow remarriage and an end to child marriage.

summary.en: Pune's public Ganesh festival began in the early 1890s, but who started it, and in which year, is still argued over. In 2017 the question became a public dispute.

en.text: In 2017 the Pune Municipal Corporation prepared to mark 125 years of the community Ganesh festival, crediting Bal Gangadhar Tilak and the year 1893.

The Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari Ganapati Trust argued that Bhausaheb Laxman Jawale, known as Bhau Rangari, organised the first public celebration in 1892, with three idols installed in different parts of the city. It said Tilak's own first public idol came in 1894, and cited a government reference book on freedom fighters.
The then mayor, a descendant of Tilak, held to 1893 and Tilak's role in encouraging public participation, citing J. S. Karandikar's 1957 history of the festival among other evidence.
A historian quoted in the same report suggested that police permission records from 1892–93 could settle the question. PunePedia has not seen those records.

title.en: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute is founded

summary.en: BORI was founded on 6 July 1917 in honour of R. G. Bhandarkar. Two years later it began its critical edition of the Mahabharata.

en.text: The decision to found the institute was taken at a meeting in Pune on 6 July 1915, and it was founded on 6 July 1917 to honour Sir Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar.

The Government of Bombay's manuscript collection was transferred to the institute on 1 April 1918. Work on the critical edition of the Mahabharata was inaugurated on 1 April 1919, and its completion was announced on 22 September 1966 by President Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan.

The Poona Pact was signed at Yerwada Central Jail on 24 September 1932. B. R. Ambedkar signed for the Depressed Classes and Madan Mohan Malaviya for the Hindus. It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats within joint electorates.
